p: Wednesday, December 16. Sunset at 4:37, civil twilight over at 5:07, and at 5:12 Biscuit started rolling, which Abby had timed down to the minute so the whole flight would go in the night column with nobody arguing about it.

Runup on Alpha near the end of 35 Right. Mags, carb heat, both door latches, and the top one on her side twice. She told ground she was ready for departure, and ground told her to monitor tower. Abby had both hands around a thermos, and as far as Jordan could tell she didn't touch the controls once in two hours.

It was a half moon, a little less, high in the south and bright enough to put shadows under the wing struts on the ramp. South of the shelf Abby had her climb to nine thousand five hundred, and the I-25 headlights ran out ahead of them over Castle Rock and Larkspur and up Monument Hill, every one of them sharp. Three nights ago this ridge had been under a gray lid. Tonight it was a ridge with a highway on it, and she watched the highway the whole way over the top anyway.

Pueblo tower cleared them to land at 5:56. On the ramp, through the FBO window, she could see a woman in a quilted coat holding a foil-covered pan with both hands like a casserole at a funeral, which was her aunt, who'd driven out to the airport because Jordan's mother had called her. The flan had the burnt part on top. Abby ate two pieces standing up in the lobby and said it was the best dispatch release she'd ever been handed.
Jordan called her mother from the ramp, in the cold, with the beacon going white and green over her head.
I know. Your tia called me from the parking lot. A pause. Was it a good flight?
It was a clear flight. Which was the honest answer, and her mother seemed to understand it was a different thing from a beautiful night. Call me from Centennial. Not the car. Centennial.

Home at ten thousand five hundred, two full stops, 7:50 at the tie down. Two point oh, all of it night, 160 nautical miles. In the logbook, under the night line, Abby drew a box and put a check in it with the green pen, and then she capped the pen and looked at Jordan over the wing.
That's the night. Book the written. January. Text me the date before you click anything.
Abby's Ground School: the rules, and the room you take them in.

Here's the test, straight from the FAA's testing matrix, the version revised in September. The Private Pilot Airplane test, code PAR, is 60 questions in 2.0 hours, and you pass with 70 percent. That's 42 right. Every question has three choices. The FAA also slips in a few validation questions it's trying out. They don't count for or against you, you can't tell which ones they are, and the two hours already includes the time to answer them. So answer every question like it counts.

You'll see 2.5 hours in older books. You'll even see it in a table at the back of the private pilot ACS. The FAA cut the time for this test on April 24, 2023, and the matrix is the newer document. It says two. When two FAA papers disagree about a number, look at the dates.

Some questions need a chart or a graph. Some of those now show the picture right on the screen with the question, because the FAA and PSI, the company that runs knowledge testing for it, have been building the images into the questions. Others still send you to the supplement book, FAA-CT-8080-2H, the Airman Knowledge Testing Supplement for Sport Pilot, Recreational Pilot, Remote Pilot, and Private Pilot. It's from 2018, and some of its sectional excerpts are printed small enough to make a grown woman squint. The proctor hands it to you and takes it back, and checks it for marks, so don't write in it. The FAA says the books stay in the testing centers until it announces a removal date, with plenty of notice.
Two hours for sixty questions is two minutes each. Most of them take thirty seconds. The ones with a figure take five minutes. It comes out about even, and you'll have time left if you don't stall.
How the exam asks it. Passing is 70 percent. If a book says 2.5 hours, the book is old.

Three things get you a seat. The first is an FAA Tracking Number. You got one in May, when we did your student certificate in IACRA, and it prints on your score report. You register with it on PSI's website and pick a testing center.

The second is identification. 61.35 wants a photograph, a signature, and a date of birth that shows you'll meet the age requirement before the report expires. The matrix adds that the ID has to be valid and current and show your physical residential address. A Colorado driver's license with your apartment on it does all of that. A post office box isn't a residential address. If your license doesn't show where you live, the matrix lists other proof you can bring, like a utility bill or a signed lease. Read the list before you go, because not every bill counts.

The third is authorization. 61.35(a)(1) says you need an endorsement from an instructor that you've done the ground training or a home-study course and you're prepared. 61.103(d) says it again from the private pilot side. AC 61-65K has the wording in Appendix A. For your test it's A.36: I certify you've received the training in 61.105, and I've determined you're prepared for the knowledge test. If you'd studied on your own, I could review your home study and sign A.86 instead. Either way it's my signature in your logbook, and the logbook comes with you.

61.105(b) is the list of what the test covers, thirteen items long, and it's worth reading once so nothing surprises you: the regulations, NTSB reporting, the AIM and advisory circulars, charts and navigation, radio procedures, weather, collision avoidance and wake turbulence, density altitude, weight and balance, aerodynamics and systems, stalls and spins, decision making, and preflight action including alternatives. That's the menu. You've eaten all of it.

What you can carry in: a plotter, a flight computer like an E6B, a straightedge, and a calculator, as long as you clear its memory in front of the proctor before and after. No written material of any kind, and that includes anything written on your tools. What the manufacturer printed on an E6B is fine. Your notes on it aren't. They give you scratch paper, count it out, and count it back. Bathroom breaks are allowed with an escort, and the clock keeps running while you're gone.
How the exam asks it. To take a knowledge test you need an instructor's endorsement and proper identification. Not a medical, and not a solo endorsement.
The report, and the codes on it.

When you finish, your score comes up on the screen, and the proctor prints an Airman Knowledge Test Report with an embossed seal on it. Everybody calls it the AKTR. It has your name, your FTN, your score, and a list of codes for the questions you missed. On the private test those are ACS codes.

Read one with me. PA.I.C.K2. PA is the private pilot airplane ACS. I is the area of operation, Preflight Preparation. C is the task, Weather Information. K2 is the second knowledge element in that task. The code tells you where the question came from. It doesn't tell you the question, and nobody ever will. You go back and learn the whole element.

That paper matters two more times. 61.39(a)(1) says you have to have passed the knowledge test within the 24 calendar months before the month you finish the practical test. Pass in January 2027 and you're good through January 31, 2029. And 61.39(a)(6) says that before your checkride I have to sign that you've had training within the 2 calendar months before the month you apply, that you're ready, and that you've shown me you know the areas you missed on the test. Those are endorsements A.1 and A.2. The ACS then tells the examiner that the oral has to include whatever you missed. So the codes on that report are the first page of your checkride.

Keep the original, in your logbook, not your glovebox. If you lose it, the FAA says PSI can print a duplicate for any test taken on or after January 13, 2020. Fail the test and 61.49 says you need more training from an instructor and an endorsement that you're ready, and you bring the failed report with you. Pass it and hate your score, and the matrix lets you sit it again with the passing report as your authorization, after 30 days, and you hand in the old report. The new score is the one that counts, even if it's lower. Most people find better uses for a Tuesday.
How the exam asks it. Expect the 24 calendar month window, and the instructor's review of your missed areas before the practical test.
What a private pilot can do: 61.113.
Now the regulations. You'll get more of these on the test than anything else, so we'll go slow, starting with the one you'll live under for the rest of your life.

61.113(a): a private pilot can't act as pilot in command of an aircraft carrying passengers or property for compensation or hire, and can't be paid to act as pilot in command at all. Then come the exceptions. You can fly in connection with your business or job, if the flight is only incidental to it and nobody's paying to ride or to ship something. You can fly a charitable, nonprofit, or community event flight that follows 91.146. You can be reimbursed for fuel, oil, airport costs, or rental on a search and location flight run by a government agency or a search organization. An aircraft salesman with 200 hours can demonstrate an airplane to a buyer. And paragraph (i) is BasicMed, which is a different afternoon.

Paragraph (c) is the one everybody asks about. A private pilot may not pay less than the pro rata share of the operating expenses of a flight with passengers, and the only expenses that count are fuel, oil, airport expenditures, and rental fees. Pro rata means split evenly among everyone aboard, the pilot included. Three people, you pay at least a third. You can pay more. You can't pay less.

AC 61-142 has the fine print, and it's short. Insurance, maintenance, depreciation, charts: not shareable. If it's not one of those four things, the pilot pays it. The FAA has also read the rule for decades to require a common purpose. You need your own reason to go to that place, and you're the one who picks it. Your cousin asks you to fly him to Grand Junction to get his truck, and he'll buy the gas? No common purpose. You're flying to your mother's birthday dinner and your sister-in-law rides along to the same dinner? That's one. And you can't advertise seats to the public, which the AC calls holding out. There's a line in there you'll like. Compensation doesn't have to be money. The AC lists piling up flight time as a kind of compensation. So when you're a private pilot and somebody offers you free use of their airplane if you'll just fly them to Vegas, that isn't free.
How the exam asks it. Pro rata questions are division. Add up the shareable costs, divide by everyone aboard including the pilot, and that's the least the pilot pays.
Staying legal after the checkride: 61.56 and 61.57.

61.56(c) says you can't act as pilot in command unless, since the beginning of the 24th calendar month before the month you're flying, you've done a flight review and had it endorsed. A flight review is at least an hour of ground and an hour of flight, covering the Part 91 rules and whatever maneuvers the instructor decides you need to show. Calendar months, again. A review signed any day in December 2024 is good through December 31, 2026. On January 1 it isn't.

Two outs that matter to you. A checkride counts as one, so your private checkride is your first flight review, and your 24 months start the month you pass. And 61.56(g) says a student pilot in training with a current solo endorsement doesn't need one, which is why I've never brought it up. There's a third, the WINGS program in 61.56(e), for later.

To carry anybody, 61.57(a) wants three takeoffs and three landings in the preceding 90 days, as the sole manipulator of the controls, in the same category and class, and type if a type rating is required. In a tricycle gear airplane touch and goes count. In a tailwheel airplane they have to be full stops. You know the night version from December: three takeoffs and three landings to a full stop between an hour after sunset and an hour before sunrise.

Currency is the legal floor and nothing else. The ACS asks you about proficiency versus currency, PA.I.A.R1, and you already know which one I care about. Three landings in 90 days makes it legal to take Ellie. It doesn't make you ready for a gusty crosswind at Akron.
How the exam asks it. Flight review math runs to the end of the month. A review from any day in June 2025 is good through June 30, 2027.
Medicals, what's in your pocket, and your address.

61.23 again, because the test will ask it with a different birthday. A third class medical used for private privileges lasts until the end of the 60th month after the month of the exam if you were under 40 when you took it, and the 24th month if you were 40 or older. A first or second class used for private flying follows the same 60 and 24. The higher privileges run out sooner. A first class taken at 38 is good for airline captain work for 12 months and for your kind of flying for 60.

Yours was April 2026, at 35, so it runs through April 30, 2031. Walt's last one was in March 2025, well after he turned 40, so it's on the 24 month clock and runs through the end of March 2027. He booked the next exam in December. Of course he did.

61.53 is the one people confuse with it. You can't act as pilot in command while you know or have reason to know of a medical condition that would make you unable to meet the requirements for your medical, or while you're taking a medication or getting a treatment that would. It's about disqualifying conditions and medications. Everything smaller is IMSAFE's job.

When you're pilot in command, 61.3 wants three things on you or easy to reach in the airplane: your pilot certificate, a photo ID like a driver's license, and your medical. If you fly under BasicMed, a valid U.S. driver's license takes the medical's place, and the BasicMed checklist and course certificate stay in your logbook. On a solo cross-country, 61.51(i)(2) also wants your logbook and student certificate aboard, which is why your logbook has lived in the flight bag since November. And you show your logbook to the FAA, the NTSB, or a police officer who asks reasonably. 61.51(b) is what goes in it: date, total time, where you left and landed, the aircraft type and N number, and what kind of time it was: solo, pilot in command, training received, day or night, actual or simulated instrument.

Move, and 61.60 gives you 30 days to tell the FAA's Airman Certification Branch, in writing. After that you can't use your certificate until you do. The regulation even prints the post office box in Oklahoma City, which I find kind of charming.
How the exam asks it. Medical questions give an age at the exam and a date. Find the privileges and the age, then count months to the end of the month.

91.7 is short. Nobody flies an airplane that isn't airworthy, the pilot in command decides whether it's in condition for safe flight, and the pilot ends the flight when something unairworthy shows up. You're the last inspector every single time, and Marisol's signature doesn't change that.

In the airplane, 91.203 wants the airworthiness certificate displayed at the cabin or cockpit entrance where people can read it, and an effective registration certificate. Under 47.40 a registration now lasts seven years from the last day of the month it was issued. 47.41 ends one early in a few cases: the airplane's sold, or destroyed, or 30 days have passed since the death of the person it's registered to. 91.9 wants the operating limitations, which means the approved flight manual or POH, the markings, and the placards, and then there's the weight and balance data for that exact airplane. ARROW, with the extra R, the radio station license, only needed now when you fly to another country.

Biscuit's paperwork is in the plastic sleeve on the left door post. The POH is in the seat pocket, and inside its back cover is the copy of Marisol's 2019 weight and balance you put there in August, where Danny's old 1,438 pound card used to be. The maintenance logbooks live in Marisol's cabinet, not in the airplane, which is where they belong.
How the exam asks it. Which document isn't required on board? The maintenance records. They stay in the hangar.

You did this in May with the cowling off, so here's the review. The annual, 91.409(a), within the preceding 12 calendar months, signed by an A&P with an inspection authorization. The 100 hour, 91.409(b), only if the airplane carries people for hire or someone gives flight instruction for hire in an airplane that person provides, and you can run 10 hours over to reach a shop, which comes out of the next 100. The transponder, 91.413, every 24 calendar months. The ELT, 91.207: inspected every 12 calendar months, and the battery replaced after more than one cumulative hour of use or when half its useful life is gone, with the new date marked on the outside of the unit and in the records. 91.207(f) even exempts training flights that stay within 50 nautical miles. Biscuit has one anyway, because Biscuit goes to Pueblo.

91.417 is what has to be kept. Records of maintenance and inspections, each with a description of the work, the date, and the signature and certificate number of whoever returned the airplane to service. Those can go once the work is repeated or superseded, or after a year. Then the records that live forever and go with the airplane when it's sold: total time on the airframe, engine, and propeller, the status of life-limited parts, time since overhaul, the current inspection status, and the current status of every applicable airworthiness directive, with its number and revision date, the method of compliance, and, if it recurs, when it's due next.

Part 39 calls ADs legally enforceable rules for aircraft, engines, propellers, and appliances, and 39.7 says operating a product that doesn't meet an applicable AD is a violation. A service bulletin from the manufacturer is advice. An AD is the FAA. Some are one time, some recur, and each one has a compliance time, usually hours or calendar time, whichever comes first. Inside that window the airplane's legal to fly. 91.403(a) makes the owner or operator primarily responsible for keeping the airplane airworthy, ADs included. You're an owner now. That's partly your name on the list.

After any maintenance, 91.407 says the airplane needs a return to service by someone authorized, and the logbook entry, before anybody flies it. If the work might have changed how it flies, a private pilot or better has to fly it, check it, and log it before passengers ride.
How the exam asks it. ADs are mandatory, and the owner or operator is primarily responsible for them. The pilot still decides before each flight whether the airplane is airworthy.
This one's in Title 49, not 14, and it's the one paramedics get wrong, so listen. 49 CFR 830 is the NTSB's rule on notifying and reporting.

An aircraft accident is an occurrence associated with operating an aircraft, between the time anyone boards with the intention of flight and the time everyone has gotten off, in which somebody dies or is seriously injured or the aircraft takes substantial damage. A fatal injury is one that causes death within 30 days.

Serious injury has a definition, and it isn't the one you use in the back of a rig. It means hospitalization for more than 48 hours, starting within 7 days of the injury. Or a fracture of any bone, except simple fractures of fingers, toes, or the nose. Or severe hemorrhage, or nerve, muscle, or tendon damage. Or anything involving an internal organ. Or second or third degree burns, or any burns over more than 5 percent of the body. A broken wrist is serious. A simple broken finger isn't, under 830.2, no matter what the person holding it says.

Substantial damage is damage or failure that hurts the structural strength, performance, or flight characteristics, and would normally need a major repair or replacement. Then comes the list of what doesn't count, which the test adores: an engine failure or damage limited to one engine, bent fairings or cowling, dented skin, small punctured holes, ground damage to propeller blades, and damage to landing gear, wheels, tires, flaps, engine accessories, brakes, or wingtips.

830.5 says you notify the nearest NTSB office immediately, by the fastest means you've got, of any accident and of a list of serious incidents. The ones that fit an airplane like Biscuit: a flight control system malfunction or failure, a required crewmember who can't do the job because of injury or illness, an in-flight fire, a collision in flight, damage to property other than the aircraft estimated at more than $25,000, release of all or part of a propeller blade other than from ground contact alone, and an overdue aircraft believed to be in an accident. There are more for big airplanes and glass panels. Notice what isn't on it. An engine failure by itself.

830.15 is the written report, on NTSB Form 6120.1/2, due within 10 days after an accident, or after 7 days if an overdue aircraft is still missing. For an incident on the list, you send a report only if the NTSB asks. 830.10 says preserve the wreckage and the records, and don't move anything except to get people out, to protect the wreckage, or to protect the public. If you have to move something, take photos and notes first.

One more, from Part 91. 91.25 says the FAA won't use what you send to NASA's Aviation Safety Reporting Program against you in an enforcement action, except for accidents and crimes. When you mess up and nobody gets hurt, write it down and send it. It's the grown-up version of Danny's notebook.
How the exam asks it. Expect to sort events into accident, notifiable incident, or neither. A flat tire or a dented wingtip isn't substantial damage.

Area XII is the part of the checkride nobody practices, because the flying's over. The ACS wants the shutdown and securing done by checklist, a postflight inspection, and any discrepancies and servicing needs written down. It also names the risks: distractions, the airport's security rules, and passengers wandering around a ramp full of propellers.

Here's how I want it. Before the engine stops, listen on the emergency frequency for a few seconds. The AIM says hard landings set off ELTs, and you'd rather know before you walk away than when somebody at the FBO hears it and calls Marisol. Mixture, mags, master, by the checklist. Control lock in. Chocks, then the left wing rope, the right wing, and the tail, snug but not tight as a guitar string, with knots you can untie in January with gloves on. Pitot cover. Then walk around her again like it's a preflight, because it's the next pilot's preflight. Oil, blue stains from fuel, new dents, tires.

Whatever you find goes on the squawk sheet in the binder, in words a stranger could act on, with the date and your name. If it might ground the airplane, tell Marisol and whoever has Biscuit next, tonight, not when it's convenient. Passengers get out after the propeller stops, on the side away from it, and you walk them off the ramp. The flight isn't over until the next person can trust the airplane.
How the exam asks it. Postflight is rare on the written and certain on the checkride. Know the sequence, and know discrepancies get written down.
Last part, and it's the one I wish somebody had told me. Sleep the night before. You know that. You also know your schedule. No solo the morning after a 24. Treat the written like a solo.

Read the last line of each question first, because that's the actual question. Then read the whole thing and try to answer before you look at the choices. With three choices, one is usually silly, one is close, and one is right. The close one is the trap, and it's close on purpose, often with a number borrowed from the wrong regulation.

Use the figure every time, even when you're sure you remember what it says. If a question stops you cold, choose the best answer you've got, mark it, and move on. A blank is wrong. A guess has a one in three chance.
When you've answered all sixty, go back to the marked ones. Change an answer only when you can say why, in your head, with a regulation number in the sentence. A feeling isn't a reason.

And study the reasons, not the answers. The question banks are out there and people memorize them, and then the FAA changes one number and they pick the old answer. If you can't explain why the right one is right, you don't know it yet. You just recognize it.
How the exam asks it. None of this is on the test. It's how you get through it.
Decision one. Two in the morning.

Friday, December 18, 2:10 in the morning, the station kitchen, the quiet stretch of a twenty four. The microwave clock was four minutes fast and nobody had fixed it since the summer. Jordan had the PSI site open on her phone, logged in with the FAA Tracking Number that IACRA had handed her in May with the student certificate, and a testing center picked out in an office park off Arapahoe Road, fifteen minutes from her apartment.
The January calendar for that center showed four open slots. Friday the 8th at eight in the morning. Tuesday the 12th at nine. Saturday the 23rd at one. Thursday, February 4, at ten.

Taped to the station fridge, under a magnet shaped like a defibrillator that somebody's kid had made, was the shift calendar. Her January 24s started on the 1st, the 4th, the 7th, the 10th, and the 13th, seven to seven. Abby wanted a date before Jordan clicked anything.
Wednesday night over Monument Hill she'd checked the line at the bottom of her card twice. CEILING 5,000 AGL ALL THE WAY. The ceiling had been the moon.
A. Tuesday, January 12, at nine, a full night off before it, and the week before blocked for review.
B. Don't book anything yet. Wait until Abby says she's ready, and then pick a date.
C. Friday, January 8, at eight. First open slot, and it's a short drive from the station.
D. Thursday, February 4, closer to the checkride, so all of it is still fresh for the oral.

She counts it twice on the fridge. The 10th ends at seven on the 11th, she sleeps the 11th, and the 12th is the first clear day. She blocks the 4th through the 11th in her calendar for review, around the shifts, and texts Abby the date and a screenshot. Abby answers at 6:40. Good. That's a date you'll arrive rested for. Endorsement on the 6th if you earn it.

That's it. Picking a date around her shift cycle protects sleep, and blocking the week before makes the review real. A firm date also leaves room afterward for the instructor's review of missed areas and the checkride prep before the April deadline.

Tuesday, December 22. The long one. KAPA to Limon, 57.7 miles, the leg she'd log as her one over fifty in a straight line. Limon to Pueblo, 70.8. Pueblo home, 78.6. Two hundred and seven nautical miles, three full stops, flight following on every leg, the limits from Abby's November endorsement copied onto the top of her kneeboard, and a new endorsement for today written underneath them in green.

Limon had a 4,700 foot runway, a self-serve pump that took a card, a windsock frozen stiff at a forty five degree angle, and two deer standing in the grass by the end of 34 like they'd been hired. Pueblo had a tower and a wind out of the north that made the last leg home take longer than it had any right to. She was on the ground at Centennial at 12:14, with forty six minutes to spare on Abby's one o'clock line.

At the tie down she did it the way Abby taught it. Before the engine stopped she listened on the emergency frequency for a few seconds. Nothing but hiss. Mixture, mags, master. Control lock. Chocks, left rope, right rope, tail. Pitot cover. Then the walkaround again, slowly, because tomorrow at seven it would be Walt's preflight.

The left fuel cap had a blue stain fanning back from it across the top of the wing, a thin streak of dyed fuel that had dried in the wind. She unscrewed the cap. The rubber gasket under it had a crack running halfway around. The left gauge had been reading low since Pueblo, and she'd blamed the gauge.
Inside the hangar, on the shelf under the whiteboard with Danny's capitals still on it, sat the coffee can of spare fuel caps.
A. Leave it. She landed with plenty of fuel, so the cap is doing its job well enough.
B. Swap in a cap from the coffee can. Then Biscuit's ready for Walt at seven.
C. Mention it to Marisol the next time she's around, and dip the tanks to be sure it's not a leak.
D. Write it on the squawk sheet, text Marisol a photo, and tell Walt before his seven o'clock.

She writes it in the binder in block capitals: 12/22, 1225. LEFT FUEL CAP GASKET CRACKED. FUEL STAIN AFT OF CAP ON WING. LEFT GAUGE READ LOW AFTER KPUB. J. REYES. Photo to Marisol, photo to Walt. Marisol answers in four minutes. Don't touch it. Coming. She's there in twenty, puts a new cap on from the coffee can, and writes a line in Biscuit's logbook. Danny bought that whole can at a swap meet in 2019. Said Biscuit eats fuel caps. She does. Walt texts back one word, Good., which from Walt is a medal.

Yep. That's the one. PA.XII.A: a postflight inspection, documented discrepancies, and a secured airplane. Writing the squawk so a stranger could act on it and telling the mechanic and the next pilot right away is how a postflight protects the next flight.

Friday, December 25, Claire's kitchen in Parker. Tamales steaming in the big pot, the good tablecloth, a Christmas playlist that had already looped twice. Ellie's present to Jordan had been a luggage tag for the flight bag that said PILOT IN COMMAND in silver glitter glue, which was early by at least one checkride, and which Jordan had clipped on the strap immediately.
After the dishes Claire put an envelope on the counter. On the front, in her handwriting, AKRON GAS. Inside, a stack of twenties.
For whenever it is. Danny never once let me pay for anything on that airplane. I want to pay for this one.
Ellie came in from the living room with a sandwich bag of quarters and set it on top of the envelope. Six dollars. She'd counted it twice in front of everybody.
Jordan had read 61.113 four times that week. She looked at the envelope.
A. Split everything three ways for the month they fly, the gas and her $410 share payment both.
B. Hand it back, and tell Claire she'll pay for the whole trip herself.
C. Take the envelope. Claire wants to pay, and this is Ellie's trip as much as hers.
D. Thank her, and explain it: she pays at least a third of the gas, oil, and fees.

She explains it on the back of the envelope with a pen from the junk drawer. Fuel, oil, airport fees. Three people aboard, so she pays at least a third. Claire can pay the rest of those, if she wants, but not insurance, not the monthly payment, not maintenance. Ellie reads it upside down. Do I count? I'm a person. You count. You're a third. Ellie considers this and pushes the quarters toward Claire. Then Mom pays mine. Claire laughs, the real one, the one Jordan hasn't heard since summer, and takes back two of the twenties without being asked.

Exactly right. 61.113(c): the pilot pays no less than her pro rata share, counting everyone aboard, and only fuel, oil, airport expenditures, and rental fees can be shared (AC 61-142). The trip is Jordan's own, to a place she chose, so there's a common purpose.
Monday, December 28, 9:14 AM, the club chat.
A message from Russ Kim. booked biscuit jan 1, 8 am, pancakes in pueblo with the brother in law. new years tradition starting now

A message from Russ Kim. q for the paramedic since she reads everything. my flight review was dec 2024 i think, the 12th, with the guy from the north end. two years is two years right. also i moved to lone tree nov 20, does the faa need to know or is that a vibe
Jordan was on her couch with coffee and the Part 61 printout she'd been marking up all weekend. She'd just highlighted 61.56(c) in orange.
A. Stay out of it. Russ was flying before she could drive, and catching this is Walt's job.
B. Answer in the chat: good through December 31, not on January 1, and the address clock already ran out.
C. Text Walt privately and let the safety officer bring it up with Russ.
D. Tell him he's fine until mid-January, since the 24 months run from the day the review was signed.

61.56(c): Dec 2024 review covers you through Dec 31. Jan 1 you're not current. Abby has slots. 61.60: you had 30 days to tell the FAA your new address, in writing. Nov 20 plus 30 was Dec 20. Have you flown since? Three dots for a long time. i was in phoenix. so no. Then: in WRITING. like a letter. The reg has a PO box in Oklahoma City. i'm going to mail the faa a christmas card. Abby, a minute later: Russ. Wednesday at ten. 1.0 ground, 1.0 flight. Bring donuts. That's my fee on top of my fee.

That's it. 61.56(c) runs to the end of the 24th calendar month, so a December 2024 review expires after December 31, 2026. 61.60 bars using the certificate more than 30 days after a move until the FAA is notified in writing, and notifying fixes it going forward.

Sunday, January 3, 7:40 in the morning, the hangar. Jordan had a dual lesson at nine, hood work and steep turns, the last of her three instrument hours. Russ had flown his review with Abby on the 30th and Pueblo on New Year's Day, and had brought back a box of pastries with one missing, which he swore was quality control.

Marisol had a printout on the workbench with a coffee ring already on it. An airworthiness directive, new, effective December 28, for the fuel selector valves on a range of 172s from the late seventies. Biscuit's serial number was in the range. Inspect the valve detent and the shaft seal within the next 50 hours time in service or 6 months, whichever came first, then every 100 hours.
A message from Russ Kim. is biscuit grounded? asking for me. and for the pastries
Marisol didn't look up from her coffee. Well? You're an owner. You tell me.
A. Fly. On an airplane this old, ADs are factory advice, and Marisol would have said if it mattered.
B. Fly. ADs are the owners' problem, and the pilot just flies what's on the schedule.
C. Read the AD's applicability and compliance time, check the AD record and the hours, then decide.
D. Cancel today. Nobody should fly an airplane with an open AD on the fuel selector.

She reads it like a drug insert. Applicability: Biscuit's in. Compliance: 50 hours time in service or 6 months after December 28, whichever first. June 28, then. She checks the tach against the last logbook entry. 3.0 hours since the effective date. Then the AD list in the engine logbook, where Marisol has already added it in pencil with the due column filled in. Legal until June 28 or 47 more hours. She's due Tuesday anyway? Tuesday. Because it's that valve, and because I've been wanting an excuse. Jordan types it into the chat for Russ: Not grounded. AD compliance by 6/28 or 50 hrs. Marisol's doing it Tuesday.

Yep. That's the one. ADs are mandatory (39.7), and their status must be recorded (91.417(a)(2)(v)). Checking applicability, compliance time, hours since the effective date, and the AD record shows whether the airplane is legal today. The PIC makes that call under 91.7(b).
Decision six. Show me she's legal.

11:20 AM, after the lesson. 1.2 on the Hobbs, 0.7 of it under the hood, and her instrument line in the logbook finally said 3.1. Abby sat on an upturned bucket in the hangar with her coffee and her clipboard, and tried to look like a stranger, and failed.
I'm the examiner. We've just met. Show me this airplane is airworthy and legal to fly today.

The squawk sheet was on the binder on the wing, the left fuel cap from December 22 written up and closed out. The maintenance logbooks were in Marisol's cabinet. The door post sleeve was right there, scratched and a little cloudy, the way it had been in every photo Danny ever sent.
A. Point to the hangar whiteboard and the squawk sheet, which show what's due.
B. Show the papers in the airplane, then open the maintenance logbook to the annual.
C. Hand over the club binder and say Marisol keeps all of it current.
D. ARROW in the airplane, then the logbooks, the ADs, and the squawk sheet.

Airworthiness certificate in the sleeve, readable from the door. Registration behind it. She reads the owner line before she can stop herself: HANGAR SIX FLYING CLUB LLC. Not four names. Not his. She'd looked up 47.41 at three in the morning once, the 30 days after the death of the holder, and never asked anybody. POH in the seat pocket, placards, the weight and balance in the back cover. Then the logbooks: annual August 20, 2026, M. Tran, IA, good through August 31, 2027. ELT inspected the same day, battery date on the unit from May. Transponder and static check October 7, good through October 2028. The AD list, with the selector line in pencil, due June 28. Squawk sheet, nothing open. Abby nods once. You were looking for his name. I was checking if she'd been illegal since April. Both. Fine. Both.

Exactly right. PA.I.B.S1 and S2: locate the airworthiness and registration documents, and determine airworthiness from the inspection records, AD status, and discrepancies. ARROW covers what's aboard. The logbooks cover the rest.

Wednesday, January 6, two in the afternoon, the briefing room. Abby had her own logbook open next to Jordan's and was adding in the margin again. Thirteen hundred and thirty one. Her phone buzzed once face down on the table with a number from an area code Jordan didn't know, and Abby let it buzz.
Jordan had been scoring between 94 and 98 on the practice app for a week. She'd shown Abby the screenshots. Abby had looked at them the way she looked at a landing she hadn't seen.
One question before I sign. A private pilot takes a third class medical at age 41. When does it run out for private privileges?
End of the 60th month. It came out before she'd thought about it. She heard it come out.
The app's question says 39. I said 41. You answered the app. Six days to the test.
A. Read Parts 61 and 91 straight through, cover to cover, before Tuesday.
B. Stop studying. She's scoring 96 on the app, and more cramming would only make her anxious.
C. Take every miss, hers and the app's, back to the regulation, and say the why out loud.
D. Run the app's whole question bank again until she's seen every question at least twice.

She builds a list on a legal pad, every miss from the app and from Abby's pre-solo test in October, and next to each one the section number. Then she explains each out loud to the whiteboard like it's a new EMT on their first shift. 61.23, 41 at the exam, 24th month. 830.2, hospitalized more than 48 hours. 91.417, AD status. Abby listens to six of them, stops her on one, makes her redo it, and then uncaps the green pen and signs. Explain it like that on Tuesday and the computer won't know what hit it.
That's it. Studying from the regulation, and explaining the reason out loud, builds the knowledge that survives a changed number. It's the same correlation the ACS asks for on the oral.

Monday, January 11, 7:40 PM, her kitchen. The shift that ended at seven that morning had been a long one: a fall at a care home at three in the morning, an old man with a hip, and a daughter who held his hand the whole way in. Jordan had slept until half past one and felt mostly human.
The logbook was open on the table to the page with Abby's green ink.

Jordan's logbook, endorsements. 01/06/27. I certify that Jordan E. Reyes has received the required training in accordance with 14 CFR 61.105. I have determined they are prepared for the Private Pilot Airplane knowledge test.. /s/ 01/06/27 A. Strand 3418862CFI RE 06-30-2027. 01/06/27. I certify that Jordan E. Reyes has received the required training to qualify for solo flying. I have determined that they meet the applicable requirements of 14 CFR 61.87(p) and are proficient to make solo flights in a Cessna 172N.. /s/ 01/06/27 A. Strand 3418862CFI RE 06-30-2027
On the back page, in her own handwriting, was the list she'd made in April and kept updating like a protocol card.

Jordan's logbook, back page: 61.109(a), as of 1/11/27. TOTAL 61.1 (40) DUAL 53.2 (20) SOLO 7.9 (10). 2.1 TO GO.. XC DUAL 4.4 (3) NIGHT 5.6 (3) NIGHT XC KAPA-KPUB-KAPA 160 NM 12/16 NIGHT FULL STOPS 12 (10) HOOD 3.1 (3) SOLO XC 5.1 (5) LONG SOLO XC 12/22: KAPA-KLIC-KPUB-KAPA, 207 NM, 3 FULL STOPS, KAPA-KLIC 57.7 (150 3 PTS ONE OVER 50) SOLO TOWERED: 3 T/O, 3 FULL STOP, KAPA, 10/20 CHECKRIDE PREP 3.0 WITHIN 2 CAL MONTHS: 0.0.. KNOWLEDGE TEST: 1/12.
Is it the big test tomorrow?
The written. The big one's after.
Do you need anything? A pause. I don't know what you'd need.
A. Skip studying and the bag both. Go to Claire's for dinner and stop thinking about it.
B. Twenty minutes on her weak list, pack the bag, lights out by ten.
C. Stay up with the regulations until she feels sure. She works on four hours of sleep all the time.
D. Run one more full sixty question practice test at ten, timed, to prove she's ready.

Nothing, Ma. Sleep. Then go sleep. Twenty minutes on NTSB 830 and the chart legend. Then the bag: driver's license, current address. Logbook. The FTN on a sticky note. Her nine dollar plotter. The calculator. Two E6Bs, Danny's aluminum one with the pencil dot, and a plastic one from the pilot shop, clean, because Abby had texted in December, Proctors look at E6Bs. Bring one with nothing on it. Lights out at 9:50.
Yep. That's the one. A short review of weak areas, the required documents packed, and a full night's sleep set up test day the way a good preflight sets up a flight. Rested beats crammed.

Tuesday, January 12, 8:22 AM. The testing center was on the second floor of a tan office building off Arapahoe Road, between a dentist and an insurance agent, with a small PSI sign on the door and a waiting room with four chairs and a plant that might have been plastic.

The proctor had reading glasses on a beaded chain, a cardigan with a pen clipped to the pocket, and a second pen behind her ear for backup, which Jordan respected. She looked at the driver's license, then at Jordan, then at the license for slightly too long. You cut your hair. Jordan had, in October. The DMV photo was from 2022 and had more hair in it and less of everything else. Logbook next, turned around on the counter so Abby's green ink could be read upside down, and then a photo against a white wall that Jordan figured would follow her to her grave. Phone, keys, coat, flight bag, locker 6. Locker 6 stuck. You had to hip it.

The aids went on the counter. The plotter got shoved right back. Clear that for me, the proctor said about the calculator, and Jordan did, and they both watched the little screen go to zero the way you'd watch a monitor. The plastic E6B got flipped twice and pronounced boring. Danny's weighed about four times as much, so of course it got the lamp. The proctor tipped the wind side back and forth under it until the light found the dot. Gray, smaller than a lentil, with a circle around it in the same pencil.

My brother's. From a flight. Which flight, she had no idea. She'd never asked anybody, and now there was nobody to ask, which was a thought she hadn't planned on having at a counter in an office park at 8:24 in the morning.
Can't let anything written go in, hon. Erase it or it stays in the locker. Up to you.
A. Explain it's only a dot from one of her brother's flights, and ask for an exception this once.
B. Rub the dot out with her thumb. It's a dot, and she wants his computer in there with her.
C. Put Danny's back in the locker and take the plastic one in.
D. Agree to the locker, then slip Danny's into her jacket once the proctor turns away.

It stays in the locker. She'd known she would say that since December, when Abby texted about proctors, and she'd bought the plastic one the next morning for twenty dollars from the same guy who'd tried to upsell her on the plotter. Danny's goes back in locker 6, on his notebook, dot up. Hip. Three sheets of scratch paper, counted out loud by the proctor, who says she'll count them back in, and the supplement, which has furry corners and somebody's coffee ring on the cover that predates them both.
Exactly right. She planned for this by bringing a clean flight computer, which meets the rules on aids without touching the one that matters to her. Preparation turned a hard choice into an easy one.

Question 9 had put a chart right on the screen, crisp and new, a piece of sectional with a Class D ring and a tower frequency box she was careful not to read. Question 14 sent her to the book. The supplement was spiral bound and soft at the corners from a few thousand nervous hands, and the figure was a sectional excerpt from somewhere in the middle of the country, printed in 2018 at what felt like half the size of the real thing.

What is the floor of controlled airspace over the private airport northeast of the city? She found the city. She found two airports. Neither had a name she could read without squinting. The clock in the corner of the screen said she'd been on this one for four minutes.
A. Pick the likeliest answer, mark it for review, and move on.
B. Keep hunting the figure until she finds it. It's one question, and she hates leaving one.
C. Raise her hand and ask the proctor where on the figure the airport is.
D. Leave it blank and keep going, and come back to it at the end.
She narrows it to two, picks the one that matches the shading she can see, taps the flag, and goes to 15. By 25 she's back under two minutes a question and breathing normally.
That's it. An answered, flagged question can be revisited and still counts if time runs out. Moving on protects the time budget, and coming back later often makes the figure easier.
10:20 AM. Sixty of sixty answered. The clock said forty minutes left, and the review screen showed seven flags.

She sat back. Her shoulders were up around her ears, the way they got after a long call, and she put them down on purpose. Somewhere outside the room a printer was going and a man was asking the front desk about parking validation.

The cost-sharing question had come up as number 33, three people and a gas bill, and she'd done it the way she'd done it on the back of Claire's envelope. The NTSB one had been 51, a passenger with a broken bone, and she hadn't flagged it. She'd been sure.
A. Submit now. She's done, and second-guessing only ever makes things worse.
B. Work the seven flags first, and change an answer only for a reason she can name.
C. Go through and change any answer that feels wrong to her now.
D. Start at question one and re-answer all sixty with fresh eyes.

She goes through them one at a time. Question 14, the tiny chart: with the book turned sideways under the lamp she finds the airport name this time and the shading, and changes her answer, because now she can say why. The other six she reads, works again, and leaves alone. At 10:58 she presses the button.
Yep. That's the one. Reviewing flagged items with fresh eyes catches real errors. Changing an answer only when there's a specific reason avoids trading right answers for wrong ones out of nerves.
The screen went white for a second, which was the longest second of the year so far. Then a box. A score. A word.

The proctor printed it at the front desk, ran it through a little hand press that clunked, and handed it over with the seal still warm, pressed into the middle right of the report, where you could feel it with your thumb.

Airman Knowledge Test Report. FEDERAL AVIATION ADMINISTRATION. AIRMAN KNOWLEDGE TEST REPORT. NAME: REYES, JORDAN E. FTN: C2611804. EXAM: PRIVATE PILOT AIRPLANE (PAR). EXAM DATE: 01/12/2027 TAKE: 1. SCORE: 95% GRADE: PASS [SEAL]. EXPIRATION DATE: 01/31/2029. ACS CODES FOR INCORRECTLY ANSWERED QUESTIONS:. PA.I.D.K6. PA.I.E.K2. PA.III.A.K8. DO NOT LOSE THIS REPORT
Three codes. Three questions out of sixty. She stood in the hallway outside the suite by the elevator, with her coat on and the flight bag back on her shoulder, holding the paper by the edges.
A. Sleeve the original in her logbook, and look up the codes before she drives.
B. Take a picture of it and toss the paper in the bag. PSI can print another one.
C. Fold it into her coat pocket and text everybody the score from the car.
D. Put it in the glovebox and deal with the codes later. She passed. That's what counts.

Logbook out of the bag, report into the clear sleeve inside the back cover, two photos. Then, in the car with the engine running, the ACS on her phone. PA.I.D.K6: inflight intercept procedures. PA.I.E.K2: chart symbols. PA.III.A.K8: NTSB accident and incident reporting. She reads the third one twice, and her face does something.

Exactly right. The AKTR is needed for the checkride, and the ACS codes identify the elements to restudy before the instructor's A.2 endorsement and the examiner's oral. Looking them up right away turns a score into a plan.

In the car, with the engine running and the heater roaring on her feet, she sent one text. 95. Pass. To Abby, first, because Abby had asked for the date before Jordan clicked anything and had earned the number before anybody else.
A text from Abby Strand. Of course. Send me the codes. All of them. Then go eat something that isn't from a vending machine.

She sent the codes. Then she sent the score to Walt, because he'd asked to see her logbook every month since April and this was going in it. Walt answered in under a minute, which meant he'd had the phone in his hand.
Then, a minute later: Nobody gets a ten.
She laughed out loud in the parking lot, alone, with the windows fogging up, and a woman walking to the dentist's office looked over at her and then away.
Her mother called at 11:20. First ring on Jordan's end, which was a reversal of the usual order.
Ninety five. She could hear her mother deciding whether that was good. Your brother got a hundred on his. He called me from the parking lot.
Jordan opened her mouth and closed it.
But ninety five is very good, mija. Very good. Are you eating?

She said she was going to. When her mother hung up she sat with the phone in her lap for a while. Then she reached into the back seat for the flight bag and took out the green notebook. His, after hers. She'd found the page in December, an August from eleven years ago, a month after his first solo cross-country. She'd folded the corner down without reading it and kept the rule, even on the nights it was hard. It wasn't hard today. It was strange.

Danny's logbook, a page from August, eleven years ago. Aug 27. No flying. THE WRITTEN.. 90.. Sixty questions in 41 minutes because I wanted lunch. Lady at the desk said most people use the whole two and a half hours. I said most people aren't me. She didn't laugh. Fair.. Missed six. The report lists them as codes, PLT this and PLT that, like license plates. Looked them up in the truck. Three on the sectional, the little print, I'm not old, it's small. One on the NTSB, where apparently a broken finger isn't serious, tell that to my finger. Two on whether my passengers can pay for the gas. They can't. Not all of it. Write it on your hand, Danny.. Instructor says 90's great. Instructor says that to everyone.. Called Ma, told her 100. She'll never check. Don't tell Mom.. Jordan would get a 96 and be mad about the 4.
She read it twice. Then she laughed again, a different laugh, the one that comes out when nothing's funny.

There's no such thing as a 96, she wanted to tell him. Sixty questions don't make a 96. They go 95, then 97. He'd have argued. He'd have said that's not the point, Jordo, the point is you'd be mad about it, and she'd have said the point is you can't do math, and Claire would have told them both to stop it in front of the baby.
He'd have been wrong about the number and right about the rest. She was mad about the five. She'd been mad about it since the screen went white.

And two of her three were his. The little print on the sectional. The NTSB. She knew which question it had been, the moment she read PA.III.A.K8 in the car: a passenger with a broken bone, and she'd answered it as a paramedic, because a fracture is a fracture when you're the one splinting it, and the regulation had a list of exceptions she'd read four times and then walked straight past. He'd missed it with a finger. She'd missed it with fifteen years of patients. Same question, eleven years apart, and neither of them had flagged it.

The one she'd gotten that he hadn't was the gas money. Twice, he'd missed it. She thought about Claire's envelope and Ellie's quarters, and that she'd learned it at his kitchen counter, with his daughter asking if she counted.

For thirty five years she had been the one with the better grades and he had been the one with the better stories, and the deal had always been that he got to tease her about the grades. She'd beaten him. Five points. And there was nobody to call about it except a woman who thought he'd gotten a hundred, and she wasn't going to tell her. Don't tell Mom. That was twice now. She could do it for him twice.

His E6B was in the side pocket of the bag where she'd put it back after the locker, the pencil dot with its little circle still right where he'd left it on the wind side. She didn't look at it. She knew it was there.

She put the notebook back in the bag, next to her own logbook with the report in its sleeve. Two records of the same test, and both of them honest about the score. Only one of the two people who'd taken it had told Ma the truth.
At 2:40 that afternoon, Abby's study plan came in, in three parts, the way she sent everything.

A text from Abby Strand. PA.I.D.K6, intercepts. The intercept section of the AIM and the signals, both directions. You'll explain it to me Friday like I'm a fighter pilot who's annoyed with you.. PA.I.E.K2, chart symbols. The sectional legend. Every symbol on it, on my table, with a highlighter. Bring the reading glasses you pretend you don't need.. PA.III.A.K8, NTSB. 830.2, out loud, as a lawyer and not a medic. A simple finger fracture isn't serious. I know. I know. Then I sign A.2, and the examiner gets to ask you all three anyway. That's the whole oral, plus everything else.

That night at the kitchen table she opened her logbook to the back page and, under the last line of the 61.109 list, wrote the result in pencil, small, in her capitals, the way she'd write a set of vitals she'd need to hand off later.
KNOWLEDGE TEST 1/12/27: 95. PASS. GOOD THROUGH 1/31/29.TO FIX BEFORE THE ORAL: PA.I.D.K6 INTERCEPTS. PA.I.E.K2 CHART SYMBOLS. PA.III.A.K8 NTSB.
